strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use a direct nonlinear epigraph optimization of all correlation lags, solved by SciPy SLSQP with analytic derivatives and deterministic multistart. This is materially different from the supplied pair-transfer coordinate descent and basin hopping: every solve can change all entries of h simultaneously while balancing the mass constraint, and the epigraph explicitly represents whichever lag or lags currently attain the maximum. The objective and constraints below are the evaluator’s exact finite-support quantities; do not replace them with a circular correlation, a smoothed maximum, or a surrogate.

Exact facts: the discretized objective is a maximum of 2n-1 quadratic lag functions, the feasible set is a capped simplex, and the epigraph formulation is exactly equivalent to minimizing that maximum. Products of h entries make the problem nonconvex. SLSQP supports this smooth nonlinear constrained formulation but offers only local solutions. The hypothesis is that simultaneous updates and starts transformed or perturbed from the supplied construction may escape pairwise-coordinate local minima and lower the exact score; this is not guaranteed. Preserve and score the supplied construction as a fallback, and make no claim of global optimality or of attaining the target bound.

2. Mathematical specification

For n samples let dx=2/n and h=(h[0],...,h[n-1]). The feasible set is 0<=h[i]<=1 and sum_i h[i]=n/2; this makes dx*sum(h)=1. For the NumPy full linear-correlation output, define lag k in {-(n-1),...,n-1}, i from max(0,-k) through min(n,n-k)-1, and j=i+k. Its value is

L_k(h)=dx * sum_i h[j]*(1-h[i]).

The evaluator returns C(h)=max_k L_k(h), equivalently max(np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)). The index ranges are the finite overlap at each lag; no samples outside [0,n-1] contribute. Both lag directions and the zero lag are included. Each L_k is nonnegative on the box and is generally nonconvex because it contains products of h entries.

Introduce z=(h[0],...,h[n-1],t) and solve min_z t subject to sum_i h[i]=n/2, 0<=h[i]<=1, and t-L_k(h)>=0 for every lag k. Bound 0<=t<=0.5. This t bound does not exclude an optimum: h[i]=0.5 is feasible, has zero-lag value 0.5, and every other lag has value (n-|k|)/(2n)<=0.5, so the unrestricted minimum is at most 0.5. Since every L_k is nonnegative, the lower bound on t is also safe. Minimizing t under all lag inequalities makes t equal to the maximum lag value at the solution.

For the analytic lag Jacobian, for each pair (i,j=i+k) in the stated overlap, add dx*(1-h[i]) to derivative coordinate j and add -dx*h[j] to coordinate i. Thus

partial L_k / partial h[q] = dx * (sum over pairs with j=q of (1-h[i]) - sum over pairs with i=q of h[j]).

At k=0 this reduces to dx*(1-2*h[q]). Implement repeated-coordinate accumulation correctly, for example with NumPy add.at. The Jacobian has shape (2n-1,n) in the same lag order as np.correlate. For g_k=t-L_k, the SLSQP inequality Jacobian row is [-grad(L_k), 1]. The mass equality Jacobian is [1,...,1,0], and the objective gradient is [0,...,0,1]. No Hessian is required by SLSQP. Do not use CVXPY as if this were a convex program.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Write one program with top-level helper functions and run(seed=42, **kwargs). Import NumPy and scipy.optimize.minimize. Keep all helpers at module top level; do not use nested functions, closures, or lambdas. Use float64 throughout and no filesystem, network, parallel, or external interaction.

3.2. Resolve n and the optional parent at runtime. Attempt to read the pre-imported initial_h_values with np.asarray(..., dtype=np.float64), without hard-coding or reconstructing its entries. Accept it as a vector only if it is one-dimensional and has 1 through 999 entries. If its length is in that range, use that length as n even if its values later fail validation. If no usable-length parent exists, use an integer kwargs value n_points in [1,999] if supplied; otherwise use n=47. Reject malformed or out-of-range requested sizes and use the default. Do not change resolution or interpolate the supplied parent.

Validate a parent for finiteness, values within [-1e-8,1+1e-8], and mass residual at most 1e-6 from n/2. If it passes, clip only these tiny bound excursions and send it through the joint capped-simplex projection below to obtain a valid parent candidate. If it fails, do not use it as a fallback or search start. In all cases create the universal fallback h_uniform=np.full(n,0.5). Keep both valid candidates and initialize the incumbent to the one with the lower exact score. If n=1, return h=[0.5] and its exact score directly; this is the only feasible value.

3.3. Implement a joint projection helper for any finite vector z of length n onto {h: 0<=h<=1, sum(h)=n/2}. Do not implement clip-then-rescale. The projection has h[i]=clip(z[i]-lambda,0,1), where lambda makes the sum n/2. Reject a wrong-shaped or nonfinite input. For numerical safety clip finite z values to [-1e6,1e6], bracket lambda by lo=min(z)-1 and hi=max(z)+1, and do 80 bisection steps. Since the clipped sum decreases with lambda, if sum(clip(z-mid,0,1))>n/2 set lo=mid; otherwise set hi=mid. Construct h using the midpoint of the final bracket. Correct any remaining sum residual by distributing it, in deterministic index order, across available upward capacities 1-h[i] or downward capacities h[i]; recompute the residual after changes. If needed, reset one fractional coordinate to n/2 minus the sum of the other coordinates when that stays in [0,1]. Return None if the final result is nonfinite, out of bounds, or has absolute mass error above 1e-10. Implement a separate feasibility predicate requiring shape (n,), finite entries, exact box bounds, and mass error at most 1e-10.

3.4. Implement exact_score(h,n). It must first reject an infeasible vector, then compute corr=np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n), reject nonfinite values or an unexpected length other than 2*n-1, and return float(np.max(corr)). This is the authoritative score for every comparison and for the return value. The pre-imported evaluator need not be called because its signature is unspecified; the in-program calculation must match its stated formula exactly.

3.5. Implement top-level lag-value and lag-Jacobian helpers. Lag values may be computed directly with the exact np.correlate expression above. For the Jacobian, iterate k from -(n-1) through n-1, form i=np.arange(max(0,-k), min(n,n-k)) and j=i+k, and accumulate the two derivative contributions from section 2 into row k+n-1. Multiply by dx. Avoid an n-by-n-by-n pair tensor. Add top-level SLSQP functions: objective returns z[-1]; objective Jacobian is zero except for a final 1; inequality function returns z[-1]-lag_values(z[:n],n); inequality Jacobian returns the negative lag Jacobian in its first n columns and a column of ones last; equality function returns sum(z[:n])-n/2; equality Jacobian returns n ones followed by zero. Pass n through the constraint dictionaries’ args fields, not through closures.

3.6. Build a deterministic pool of feasible starting h vectors using the seeded NumPy generator. Include h_uniform and, if valid, the projected parent. Also try the parent’s reverse, complement 1-parent, and complement of its reverse; each preserves mass before numerical repair. Generate an algorithmic block vector with floor(n/2) leading ones, a 0.5 next entry when n is odd, and zeros elsewhere; generate an alternating zero/one vector and project it. Add cosine profiles 0.5+0.45*cos(2*pi*m*arange(n)/n+phase) for small integer frequencies m=1,2,3 and phases 0 and pi/2, projecting each. Add seeded Gaussian perturbations of the parent, or of h_uniform when no parent exists, with standard deviations 0.04, 0.10, and 0.20, plus a seeded uniform [0,1] vector. Project every generated vector and discard failed projections. Deduplicate candidates when their maximum absolute coordinate difference is below 1e-6.

Score the pool with exact_score. Always retain h_uniform as a solver start and retain a valid parent as a solver start when its score is at most 0.5+1e-12. Fill remaining slots with the lowest-scoring distinct candidates that also have score at most 0.5+1e-12. This screening supplies starts compatible with the t upper bound; the parent remains in the fallback comparison even if it is not a solver start. For each start h0, initialize t0=min(0.5, score(h0)+1e-9), clamp it below by zero, and form z0 by appending t0. A tiny starting constraint residual caused by rounding is acceptable.

3.7. For every selected start call scipy.optimize.minimize with method='SLSQP', the linear objective and analytic Jacobians above, bounds [(0,1)] repeated n times followed by (0,0.5), one equality constraint and one vector inequality constraint, each with its analytic Jacobian. Set options ftol=1e-10, disp=False, and maxiter from section 4. Catch solver exceptions and continue. Do not trust result.fun or result.success as a score or as the sole validity test. If result.x exists, has length n+1, and is finite, project result.x[:n] with the capped-simplex helper, then compute its exact score. A finite candidate from a solver status indicating failure may still be useful.

For each projected solver candidate, compare it to the current incumbent using exact_score. Also evaluate convex blends of a saved copy of the incumbent and that candidate at alpha=0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0. Each blend is mass-feasible in exact arithmetic; project it again to remove floating-point drift, check feasibility, and score it exactly. Test all blends against the same saved incumbent, then update once to the lowest-score valid candidate. Accept only a score below the incumbent by more than 1e-12. Never accept based on the epigraph t, a surrogate, or a solver-reported objective alone.

After the initial starts, run the bounded number of refinement restarts in section 4. At each restart perturb the current best h by seeded Gaussian noise at the current sigma, project it, and use it only if its exact score is at most 0.5+1e-12 and it is not a duplicate of the incumbent. Allow at most three attempts to obtain such a start; if none is obtained, skip that restart. Optimize it with the same complete epigraph SLSQP formulation and candidate processing. Shrink or widen sigma according to whether that restart produced an exact-score improvement, using the explicit rule in section 4. This adaptation must occur inside run.

3.8. Before returning, project the incumbent once more and recheck feasibility and exact score. If projection fails, use the best of the separately retained valid parent and h_uniform; if neither is usable, use h_uniform. Compare the final projected candidate to the valid fallback candidates by exact score and keep the lowest-scoring feasible vector. Return a float64 NumPy vector, its recomputed exact float score, and int(n), in that order. Do not print a proposed score or solution.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use these defaults without preliminary experiments. For n=1 use the direct return described above. For 2<=n<=64 use up to 8 initial SLSQP starts, 4 refinement restarts, and maxiter=220 per solve. For 65<=n<=128 use up to 5 initial starts, 2 refinement restarts, and maxiter=150. For 129<=n<=999 use up to 3 initial starts, 1 refinement restart, and maxiter=80. Use ftol=1e-10 at every size. All solves are sequential on the available single CPU. The initial pool is allowed to contain more candidates than the start budget; retain the parent and uniform when eligible, then fill by lowest exact score while preserving distinctness.

For refinement initialize sigma=0.04. After a restart that lowers the incumbent by more than 1e-12, set sigma=max(0.01,0.7*sigma); after a restart without improvement or a skipped restart, set sigma=min(0.20,1.5*sigma). Use the new current incumbent for the next perturbation. Keep the three-attempt limit and the score screen in section 3. These are explicit result-dependent operations, not instructions to tune outside the program.

The correctness requirements are the full lag set, exact score acceptance, joint feasibility projection, parent fallback, and SLSQP constraints and derivatives. Permissible implementation variations are to choose starts using a diversity quota across the parent, cosine, and noise families rather than pure score ranking, to use one through four cosine frequencies, or to select noise scales within 0.02 to 0.25. A coder may modestly change the start and restart budgets or use ftol between 1e-9 and 1e-12, but should keep the defaults above for a no-experiment implementation. Any alternative schedule must remain deterministic under seed and retain a finite hard cap on solver calls. Do not replace the exact epigraph objective with a smoothed-max objective unless its output is still judged and accepted only by the exact evaluator; the specified default uses no smoothing.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64, finite checks at each input and candidate boundary, and dx=2.0/n. The products in every lag lie in [0,1] for feasible h, and the analytic derivative contributions are bounded, so no special scaling beyond dx is needed. The projection’s monotone bisection and residual correction enforce box and mass constraints jointly. Do not repair feasibility by clipping followed by scalar rescaling. Reject nonfinite solver vectors; catch solver exceptions; skip invalid projections and nonfinite exact scores. Retain h_uniform, whose exact score is 0.5, as an always-valid fallback, and retain a validated repaired parent as another fallback.

The lag vector has length 2n-1. The explicit Jacobian has (2n-1)*n float64 entries: about 35 KB at n=47 and about 16 MB at n=999. Compute it one call at a time and do not store pairwise or cubic tensors. The exact correlation and Jacobian work are O(n^2); SLSQP is dense, so the start and iteration budgets decrease with n. No parallel work is appropriate for the one-CPU harness. Reject parent or requested resolutions above 999 and fall back to the default 47-point problem rather than allocating an unbounded dense optimization. Keep the parent’s resolution when it is accepted; do not compare scores across changed resolutions.

Terminate after the fixed initial-start and refinement budgets, or earlier only for an input failure or solver exception that leaves no further work. Use SLSQP’s ftol and maxiter as its internal stopping settings; do not wait for a global-optimality certificate. A failed or early-stopped solve is handled by inspecting any finite returned vector, restoring feasibility, and exact-scoring it. If no solve improves anything, return the best valid parent/uniform fallback. These rules provide a valid output without execution-time intervention by the coder.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated run function must itself parse seed and kwargs, read and validate the optional initial_h_values global, derive n, generate starts, restore feasibility, execute bounded optimization calls, and compute all scores. Convert seed to an integer for np.random.default_rng; if conversion or generator construction fails, use seed 42. Do not assume the parent or a solver result is feasible. Check every returned candidate’s dimension, finiteness, box bounds, and mass before scoring it. For scoring, use exactly max(np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)); reject a nonfinite correlation vector. Recompute the selected candidate’s score immediately before return so the scalar corresponds to the returned h.

Maintain the best candidate only when it passes feasibility and has a finite exact score; update only for a strict improvement greater than 1e-12. If an optimization call fails, continue with other starts. If final validation fails or no candidate survives, return h=np.full(n,0.5), its exact score, and n. If a valid parent scores better than this universal fallback, it must remain eligible for return. The required interface is run(seed=42, **kwargs) returning (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, c5_bound a Python float, and n_points a Python int. The program must not claim that it has already run, measured a score, or verified an improvement.
